```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Against a 90-day first-payment target, A has the faster path. A solo founder can reach small marketplaces, dating apps and review sites through self-serve developer channels. The brief estimates $200–$500 for a Product Hunt-style launch, with no sales team needed.",
    "A's competitors publish self-serve tiers (not.bot from $9.99/mo, useHUMA up to $499/mo). That shows small platforms buy this kind of product without procurement, so a first paying customer does not depend on enterprise sales.",
    "B's own brief documents a near-identical precedent, Cydoc, that failed. It reached four paying customers over about seven years and $27,900 in 2024 revenue, mostly non-subscription. It carried $4,000–$6,000 integration cost per practice, and customers renegotiated scope for each practice. This is direct evidence that the path to a first payment is slow.",
    "B carries per-customer overhead before any revenue: a HIPAA BAA for each customer, ongoing safeguards, an FDA non-device legal review, and physician trust in liability-bearing notes. Its suggested channel, conference booths at $3,000–$10,000, is costly and slow for one person.",
    "A has serious weaknesses. Banks, Zoom-scale and other enterprise buyers are out of reach, the self-serve segment has free-tier competitors pushing prices toward zero, and biometric regulatory risk exists. Even so, A's weaknesses mostly cap its upside. B's evidence directly undercuts the 90-day goal."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's Case For claims that funded competitors charging $99–$500/provider/month have 'apparent traction, proving willingness to pay.' No source is cited for any traction. The brief supports only list prices (ClaireMed, S10.AI), and the other three competitors have no public pricing. The core willingness-to-pay argument is therefore effectively unsourced. B's direct demand quote is also weak: it comes from a PMHNP asking an employer for more paperwork, not from a practice owner who would pay.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. A's demand evidence is also thin. Its quotes come from an end user who is not the payer, from a competitor executive, and from a bank-fraud anecdote about a segment A cannot reach. A's case also depends on winning a buyer away from free-tier competitors, and its biometric/BIPA exposure is unresolved. A wins mainly because B's brief contains strong direct evidence of failure on this timeline, not because A's demand is well proven."
}
```
